results.claim: For w=(2,7,4,8,1,6,3,5), complete rook placements correspond bijectively to perfect matchings between 14 across words and 14 down words.
results.proof_sketch: Write L_i and R_i for the white words left and right of the black cell in row i, and U_j and D_j for those above and below the black cell in column j; omit empty words. Six rows have two words and two rows have one, giving 14 across words. The same holds for columns. Each white cell belongs to exactly one across word and one down word, and any such pair intersects in at most one cell. Thus selecting exactly one cell in every word is precisely selecting a perfect matching in their incidence graph.

results.claim: Every complete placement for this permutation contains (1,1), (2,8), (8,3), (1,7), and (2,4).
results.proof_sketch: The first four cells are respectively the singleton words L_1, R_2, D_3, and U_7. The word U_4 consists of (1,4) and (2,4). Since (1,7) already occupies R_1, the cell (1,4) cannot be selected. Therefore (2,4) must be selected. These five cells occupy distinct across words and distinct down words.

results.claim: Deleting the five forced matching edges and their incident words leaves a nine-by-nine incidence graph with the neighborhoods listed below, without changing the number of complete placements.
results.proof_sketch:
Label the remaining across words A=L_3, B=R_3, C=L_4, D=R_5, E=L_6, F=R_6, G=L_7, H=R_7, I=R_8. Number the remaining down words (D_1,D_2,U_3,D_4,U_5,U_6,D_6,D_7,D_8) by 1,...,9. Direct intersection gives:
A:{2,3}; B:{5,6,8}; C:{2,3,4,5,6,8}; D:{2,3,4,5,6,8,9}; E:{1,2,3,4,5}; F:{8,9}; G:{1,2}; H:{4,5,7,8,9}; I:{7,8,9}.
Every original matching restricts to a matching here. Conversely, adjoining the five forced edges extends every residual perfect matching uniquely.

results.claim: Define T(p,q) as the number of matchings of rows B,C,D,E,H onto columns {p,4,5,6,q}. The desired count is the sum, over p=1,2,3, of 2T(p,7)+T(p,8)+T(p,9).
results.proof_sketch: Rows A and G occupy two columns of {1,2,3}. Their possible assignments (A,G)=(2,1),(3,1),(3,2) leave p=3,2,1 respectively, each once. Rows F and I occupy two columns of {7,8,9}. Assignments (F,I)=(8,9),(9,8) leave q=7; (9,7) leaves q=8; and (8,7) leaves q=9. These choices involve disjoint row and column sets. After them, exactly rows B,C,D,E,H and columns {p,4,5,6,q} remain, proving the formula.
Among the remaining rows B,C,D,E,H, columns 2 and 3 have the same neighborhood, namely {C,D,E}. Relabeling column 2 as column 3 therefore gives the required bijection.

Column 1 forces E to column 1, and column 7 forces H to column 7. On columns {4,5,6}, row B has two choices, 5 or 6, while C and D can occupy the other two columns in either order. Hence the count is 2·2=4.
Column 1 forces E to column 1. On the four remaining columns {4,5,6,8}, rows B,C,D,H allow every assignment except B→4 and H→6. Inclusion–exclusion gives 4!−3!−3!+2!=14.

Column 1 forces E to column 1. Column 9 can be occupied only by D or H. If H→9, rows B,C,D match {4,5,6} in four ways. If D→9, rows B,C,H match {4,5,6}: B→5 leaves one possibility, while B→6 leaves two. The total is 4+1+2=7.

Column 7 forces H→7. The remaining columns are {2,4,5,6}. If B→5, row E has two choices, 2 or 4, followed by two assignments for C,D, giving four. If B→6, row E has three choices, followed by two assignments for C,D, giving six. Thus T(2,7)=4+6=10.

On columns {2,4,5,6,8}, rows C and D allow every column. Choose distinct columns for B,E,H first. Their allowed sets are {5,6,8}, {2,4,5}, and {4,5,8}. For B→5 there are three compatible ordered choices for E,H; for B→6 there are 3·3−2=7; for B→8 there are 3·2−2=4. Rows C,D can occupy the remaining columns in two orders. Hence the count is 2(3+7+4)=28.

Column 9 can be occupied only by D or H. If H→9, the remaining matching problem is the one counted by T(2,7), giving ten. If D→9, rows B,C,E,H match {2,4,5,6}. When B→5, the assignment C→6, E→2, H→4 is forced. When B→6, H has two choices, 4 or 5, and C,E occupy the other two columns in either order, giving four. Thus T(2,9)=10+1+4=15.

results.claim: The recorded equivalence is false: |RP(Grid(2,7,4,8,1,6,3,5))|=155, although 155≡3 modulo 4.
results.proof_sketch: The minor table, with rows p=1,2,3 and columns q=7,8,9, is [[4,14,7],[10,28,15],[10,28,15]]. Therefore the number of complete placements is (2·4+14+7)+2(2·10+28+15)=29+63+63=155. This positive integer is realized by a permutation grid but lies in a residue class excluded by the proposed equivalence.

final_writeup:
The equivalence is false. A counterexample is w=(2,7,4,8,1,6,3,5) in S_8, for which the number of complete placements is 155≡3 modulo 4. The following gives an explicit counting certificate.

Write L_i and R_i for the nonempty white words left and right of the black cell in row i, and U_j and D_j for those above and below the black cell in column j. There are 14 across words and 14 down words. Each white cell identifies an edge between its across and down words, so complete placements correspond bijectively to perfect matchings of this incidence graph.

Four cells are immediately forced: (1,1), (2,8), (8,3), and (1,7), because they are respectively the singleton words L_1, R_2, D_3, and U_7. The down word U_4 consists of (1,4) and (2,4). The first of these cannot be selected because (1,7) already occupies R_1. Consequently (2,4) is also forced.

Remove the five forced edges and their incident words. Number the remaining down words as follows:

| Number | Down word |
|---|---|
| 1 | D_1 |
| 2 | D_2 |
| 3 | U_3 |
| 4 | D_4 |
| 5 | U_5 |
| 6 | U_6 |
| 7 | D_6 |
| 8 | D_7 |
| 9 | D_8 |

The remaining across words have these neighborhoods:

| Row label | Across word | Allowed column numbers |
|---|---|---|
| A | L_3 | 2,3 |
| B | R_3 | 5,6,8 |
| C | L_4 | 2,3,4,5,6,8 |
| D | R_5 | 2,3,4,5,6,8,9 |
| E | L_6 | 1,2,3,4,5 |
| F | R_6 | 8,9 |
| G | L_7 | 1,2 |
| H | R_7 | 4,5,7,8,9 |
| I | R_8 | 7,8,9 |

Every perfect matching of this residual graph extends uniquely by adjoining the five forced edges.

Rows A and G use two columns from {1,2,3}. Each possible unused column p occurs in exactly one assignment: (A,G)=(3,2),(3,1),(2,1) leave p=1,2,3 respectively. Rows F and I use two columns from {7,8,9}. The unused column q=7 occurs twice, from assignments (8,9) and (9,8); q=8 and q=9 each occur once, from (9,7) and (8,7).

Let T(p,q) count matchings of rows B,C,D,E,H onto columns {p,4,5,6,q}. It follows that the full count is the sum over p=1,2,3 of 2T(p,7)+T(p,8)+T(p,9). The required table is

| p | T(p,7) | T(p,8) | T(p,9) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 4 | 14 | 7 |
| 2 | 10 | 28 | 15 |
| 3 | 10 | 28 | 15 |

Here is a direct verification of every distinct entry. For p=1, column 1 forces E→1. If q=7, H→7 is also forced, leaving two choices for B and two orders for C,D: four matchings. If q=8, the remaining four-by-four board permits all entries except B→4 and H→6, giving 4!−2·3!+2!=14. If q=9, assigning H→9 gives four matchings; assigning D→9 gives three, according to B→5 or B→6 contributing one or two. Thus the first row is (4,14,7).

For p=2 and q=7, H→7 is forced. Choosing B→5 gives two choices for E and two orders for C,D; choosing B→6 gives three choices for E and two orders for C,D. This gives 4+6=10.

For p=2 and q=8, C and D allow all five columns. First assign B,E,H to distinct columns. The choices B→5, B→6, B→8 leave respectively three, seven, and four possible assignments for E,H. The other two columns can be assigned to C,D in two orders, giving 2(3+7+4)=28.

For p=2 and q=9, column 9 belongs to D or H. Choosing H→9 gives ten matchings, as in the preceding q=7 calculation. Choosing D→9 gives five: one when B→5, and four when B→6. Hence the entry is 15. Finally, columns 2 and 3 have identical neighborhoods among B,C,D,E,H, so the p=3 row equals the p=2 row.

The number of complete placements is therefore (2·4+14+7)+2(2·10+28+15)=155. Since 155≡3 modulo 4, this explicit permutation disproves the proposed spectrum.
checks_performed: Created and ran rook_spectrum_check.py in the authorized scratch directory. Its exact-integer subset dynamic program enumerated all 46,233 permutations of sizes 1 through 8.

Cross-checked every permutation of size at most 5 using an independent recursion that constructs maximal white segments directly and selects cells. This independent method also returned 155 for the counterexample.
Created and ran counterexample_certificate.py. It verified the 14-by-14 word graph, each forced edge, the residual neighborhoods, and the conditioning multiplicities.

Enumerated all 120 column permutations for each of the nine five-by-five minors and all 362,880 column permutations for the residual nine-by-nine graph. The weighted minor sum, residual permanent, original subset dynamic program, and original cell-level recursion all returned 155.
